danish.title: Femtende bog (1812–13) — Kapitel 17
paragraphs: Pierre blev vist ind i den store, klart oplyste spisesal; få minutter senere hørte han skridt, og fyrstinde Marja trådte ind med Natasja. Natasja var rolig, skønt et strengt og alvorsfuldt udtryk atter havde lagt sig over hendes ansigt. Alle tre oplevede nu den følelse af akavethed, der sædvanligvis følger efter en alvorlig og inderlig samtale. Det er umuligt at vende tilbage til det samme emne, at tale om ubetydeligheder føles forkert, og dog er trangen til at tale der, mens tavshed virker kunstlet. De gik tavse til bords. Tjenerne trak stolene ud og skubbede dem ind igen. Pierre foldede sin kolde serviet ud og besluttede sig for at bryde tavsheden, idet han så på Natasja og fyrstinde Marja. De havde begge tydeligvis truffet den samme beslutning; begges øjne strålede af tilfredshed og en erkendelse af, at livet rummer glæde såvel som sorg.
»Drikker De brændevin, greve?« spurgte fyrstinde Marja, og de ord forjog med ét fortidens skygger. »Fortæl os nu om Dem selv,« sagde hun. »Man hører så utrolige ting om Dem.«

»Ja,« svarede Pierre med det mildt ironiske smil, der nu var blevet ham en vane. »De fortæller mig endda undere, jeg aldrig selv drømte om! Marja Abramovna inviterede mig hjem til sig og fortalte mig, hvad der var sket — eller burde have sket — med mig. Stepan Stepanytj belærte mig også om, hvordan jeg burde fortælle om mine oplevelser. Generelt har jeg bemærket, at det er meget let at være en interessant mand (jeg er en interessant mand nu); folk inviterer mig ud og fortæller mig alt om mig selv.«
Natasja smilede og var ved at sige noget.
»Vi har fået at vide,« afbrød fyrstinde Marja hende, »at De mistede to millioner i Moskva. Er det sandt?«
»Men jeg er tre gange rigere end før,« svarede Pierre.
Skønt hans stilling nu var ændret ved hans beslutning om at betale sin kones gæld og genopbygge sine huse, fastholdt Pierre stadig, at han var blevet tre gange rigere end før.
»Hvad jeg helt sikkert har vundet, er frihed,« begyndte han alvorligt, men fortsatte ikke, da han bemærkede, at emnet var for egocentrisk.
»Og bygger De op igen?«
»Ja. Savjelitj siger, jeg skal!«

»Sig mig, vidste De ikke om grevindens død, da De besluttede at blive i Moskva?« spurgte fyrstinde Marja og rødmede straks, da hun bemærkede, at hendes spørgsmål — efter hans omtale af frihed — tillagde hans ord en mening, han måske ikke havde tilsigtet.

»Nej,« svarede Pierre, tilsyneladende uden at finde den mening akavet, som fyrstinde Marja havde lagt i hans ord. »Jeg hørte om det i Orjol, og De kan ikke forestille Dem, hvor det rystede mig. Vi var ikke et mønsterpar,« tilføjede han hurtigt med et blik på Natasja, idet han på hendes ansigt bemærkede nysgerrighed efter, hvordan han ville tale om sin kone, »men hendes død rystede mig forfærdeligt. Når to mennesker skændes, har de altid begge skyld, og ens egen skyld bliver pludselig forfærdelig alvorlig, når den anden ikke mere er i live. Og så en sådan død... uden venner og uden trøst! Jeg beklager hende meget, meget,« sluttede han og glædede sig ved at bemærke et udtryk af glad bifald i Natasjas ansigt.
»Ja, og så er De atter ungkarl og bejler,« sagde fyrstinde Marja.

Pierre rødmede pludselig dybt karmoisinrødt og forsøgte længe ikke at se på Natasja. Da han vovede at kaste et blik i hendes retning, var hendes ansigt koldt, strengt og — syntes han — endda foragteligt.
»Og så De virkelig Napoleon og talte med ham, som vi har fået fortalt?« spurgte fyrstinde Marja.
Pierre lo.

»Nej, ikke én eneste gang! Alle synes at bilde sig ind, at det at være taget til fange er det samme som at være Napoleons gæst. Jeg så ham aldrig, og jeg hørte heller intet om ham — jeg var i langt ringere selskab!«
Aftensmaden var forbi, og Pierre, der i begyndelsen afslog at tale om sit fangenskab, blev gradvist ledt til det.
»Men er det sandt, at De blev i Moskva for at dræbe Napoleon?« spurgte Natasja med et svagt smil. »Jeg gættede det dengang, da vi mødtes ved Sukharev-tårnet, husker De det?«
Pierre indrømmede, at det var sandt, og blev derfra — gradvist ledt af fyrstinde Marjas spørgsmål og især af Natasjas — til at give en detaljeret beretning om sine oplevelser.

I begyndelsen talte han med den morsomme og milde ironi, der nu var ham sædvanlig over for alle og især over for sig selv, men da han kom til at beskrive de rædsler og lidelser, han havde været vidne til, blev han ubevidst revet med og begyndte at tale med den undertrykte bevægelse hos en mand, der genoplever stærke indtryk i erindringen.

Fyrstinde Marja betragtede med et blidt smil snart Pierre, snart Natasja. I hele beretningen så hun kun Pierre og hans godhed. Natasja, der lænede sig på albuen med et ansigtsudtryk, der uophørligt skiftede med beretningen, fulgte Pierre med en opmærksomhed, der aldrig vaklede — og oplevede tydeligvis selv alt det, han beskrev. Ikke blot hendes blik, men hendes udbrud og de korte spørgsmål, hun stillede, viste Pierre, at hun forstod netop det, han ønskede at formidle. Det var tydeligt, at hun forstod ikke blot, hvad han sagde, men også det, han gerne ville, men ikke kunne udtrykke i ord. Beretningen om episoden med barnet og kvinden, for hvis beskyttelse han blev arresteret, var denne: »Det var et frygteligt syn — børn forladt, nogle i flammerne... Ét blev revet bort lige for mine øjne... og der var kvinder, der fik revet deres ejendele fra sig og øreringene revet ud...« Han rødmede og blev forvirret. »Så kom en patrulje og tog alle mænd — alle dem, der ikke plyndrede — og mig med.«
»De fortæller bestemt ikke os alt; jeg er sikker på, at De gjorde noget...« sagde Natasja og tilføjede efter en pause: »...noget smukt?«
Pierre fortsatte. Da han talte om henrettelsen, ville han springe de forfærdelige detaljer over, men Natasja insisterede på, at han ikke udelod noget.
Pierre begyndte at fortælle om Karatajev (Platon Karatajev), men standsede. På dette tidspunkt var han rejst fra bordet og gik rundt i stuen med Natasja følgende ham med blikket. Så tilføjede han:
»Nej, De kan ikke forstå, hvad jeg lærte af den ulærde mand — den enkle fyr.«
»Jo, jo, fortsæt!« sagde Natasja. »Hvor er han?«
»De dræbte ham næsten for mine øjne.«
Og Pierre, med vedvarende sitren i stemmen, fortsatte med at fortælle om de sidste dage af deres tilbagetog, om Karatajevs sygdom og hans død.

Han fortalte om sine oplevelser, som han aldrig før havde genkaldt dem. Han så nu ligesom en ny mening i alt, hvad han havde gennemlevet. Nu da han fortalte det hele til Natasja, oplevede han den glæde, en mand føler, når kvinder lytter til ham — ikke kloge kvinder, der under lytningen enten forsøger at huske det, de hører, for at berige deres sind og gengive det ved lejlighed, eller som ønsker at tilpasse det til en egen tanke og straks bidrage med deres egne snedige kommentarer, forberedt i deres lille mentale værksted — men den glæde, ægte kvinder skænker, der er udstyret med evnen til at udvælge og opsuge det allerbedste, en mand viser af sig selv. Natasja var uden at vide det lutter opmærksomhed: hun tabte ikke et ord, ikke et enkelt skælven i Pierres stemme, ikke et blik, ikke en muskeltrækken i hans ansigt, ikke en eneste gestus. Hun greb det ufærdige ord i flugten og bar det lige ind i sit åbne hjerte, idet hun anede den hemmelige mening bag al Pierres åndelige kamp.

Fyrstinde Marja forstod hans beretning og følte med ham, men hun så nu noget andet, der opslugte al hendes opmærksomhed. Hun så muligheden for kærlighed og lykke mellem Natasja og Pierre, og den første tanke herom fyldte hendes hjerte med glæde.
Klokken var tre om morgenen. Tjenerne kom ind med alvorlige og strenge ansigter for at skifte lysene, men ingen lagde mærke til dem.

Pierre afsluttede sin fortælling. Natasja fortsatte med at betragte ham indtrængende med lyse, opmærksomme og levende øjne, som om hun forsøgte at forstå noget mere, som han måske havde undladt at fortælle. Pierre kastede i undseelig og lykkelig forvirring lejlighedsvis et blik i hendes retning og forsøgte at finde på, hvad han skulle sige næst for at dreje samtalen over på et nyt emne. Fyrstinde Marja tav. Det faldt ingen af dem ind, at klokken var tre, og at det var på tide at gå i seng.

»Man taler om ulykker og lidelser,« bemærkede Pierre, »men hvis man i dette øjeblik spurgte mig: 'Ville du hellere være, som du var, før du blev taget til fange, eller gennemleve alt dette igen?' — så for Guds skyld, lad mig igen opleve fangenskab og hestekød! Vi forestiller os, at når vi kastes ud af vores vante spor, er alt tabt, men det er netop da, det nye og gode begynder. Så længe der er liv, er der lykke. Der er meget, meget foran os. Det siger jeg til Dem,« tilføjede han og vendte sig mod Natasja.
»Ja, ja,« sagde hun og svarede på noget helt andet. »Også jeg ville ønske kun at gennemleve alt forfra.«
Pierre så indtrængende på hende.
»Ja, og intet andet,« sagde Natasja.
»Det er ikke sandt, ikke sandt!« udbrød Pierre. »Jeg kan ikke gøre for, at jeg lever og ønsker at leve — og det kan De heller ikke.«
Pludselig bøjede Natasja hovedet, skjulte ansigtet i hænderne og begyndte at græde.
»Hvad er der, Natasja?« sagde fyrstinde Marja.
»Ingenting, ingenting.« Hun smilede til Pierre gennem tårerne. »Godnat! Det er sengetid.«
Pierre rejste sig og tog afsked.
Fyrstinde Marja og Natasja mødtes som sædvanlig i soveværelset. De talte om det, Pierre havde fortalt. Fyrstinde Marja sagde ikke sin mening om Pierre, og Natasja talte heller ikke om ham.
»Nå, godnat, Marja!« sagde Natasja. »Ved du, jeg er ofte bange for, at vi ved ikke at tale om ham« — hun mente fyrst Andrej — »af frygt for ikke at yde vores følelser retfærdighed, glemmer ham.«
Fyrstinde Marja sukkede dybt og erkendte dermed rigtigheden af Natasjas bemærkning, men hun udtalte ikke sin enighed i ord.
»Er det muligt at glemme?« sagde hun.

»Det gjorde mig så godt at fortælle om det i dag. Det var hårdt og smerteligt, men godt, meget godt!« sagde Natasja. »Jeg er sikker på, at han virkelig holdt af ham. Derfor fortalte jeg ham det... Var det i orden?« tilføjede hun og rødmede pludselig.
»At fortælle Pierre? Jo, absolut. Sikke en pragtfuld mand, han er!« sagde fyrstinde Marja.

»Ved du, Marja...« sagde Natasja pludselig med et skælmsk smil, som fyrstinde Marja ikke havde set på hendes ansigt i lang tid, »han er på en eller anden måde blevet så ren, glat og frisk — som om han lige var kommet ud af et russisk bad; forstår du? Ud af et moralsk bad. Er det ikke rigtigt?«
»Ja,« svarede fyrstinde Marja. »Han er forbedret betragteligt.«
»Med en kort frakke og klippet hår; præcis som om — ja, som om han kom lige fra badet... Far plejede at...«
»Jeg forstår, hvorfor han« — hun mente fyrst Andrej — »ikke holdt af nogen så meget som af ham,« sagde fyrstinde Marja.
»Ja, og alligevel er han helt anderledes. De siger, at mænd er venner, når de er helt forskellige. Det må være sandt. Han ligner ham virkelig slet ikke — i noget.«
»Jo, men han er vidunderlig.«
»Nå, godnat,« sagde Natasja.
Og det samme skælmske smil dvælede længe på hendes ansigt, som var det blevet glemt dér.

english.title: Book Fifteen (1812 - 13) — Chapter 17
paragraphs: Pierre was shown into the large, brightly lit dining room. A few minutes later he heard footsteps, and Princess Mary entered with Natasha. Natasha was calm, though a serious, solemn expression had settled on her face again. Princess Mary, Natasha, and Pierre all equally felt that awkwardness that usually follows a serious and deeply felt conversation. To continue from where you left off is impossible; to talk about trivial things feels wrong; yet to sit in silence is unpleasant, because you want to be talking and this silence feels like pretending. They went to the table in silence. The servants pulled back their chairs and pushed them in. Pierre unfolded his cold napkin and, deciding to break the silence, glanced at Natasha and Princess Mary. Both had clearly reached the same decision at the same moment: in both their eyes shone satisfaction with life and an acknowledgment that besides grief there is also joy.
"Do you drink vodka, Count?" asked Princess Mary, and those words instantly banished the shadows of the past. "Now tell us about yourself," she said. "We hear such incredible stories about you."

"Yes," Pierre replied with the smile of mild irony that had become habitual. "People even tell me about wonders I never dreamed of! Maria Abramovna invited me over and kept telling me what had happened to me, or what should have happened. Stepan Stepanych also taught me how I ought to tell my story. In general, I've noticed that being an interesting person is very convenient"—he smiled at Natasha—"because people invite me out and then tell me everything themselves."
Natasha smiled and was about to speak.
"We've been told," Princess Mary interrupted, "that you lost two million rubles in Moscow. Is that true?"
"But I'm three times richer than before," Pierre replied.
Though his financial position had actually worsened—he'd decided to pay his wife's debts and rebuild his houses—Pierre still maintained that he was three times richer than before.
"What I've definitely gained is freedom," he began seriously, but stopped, sensing this was too self-centered a topic.
"And are you rebuilding?"
"Yes. Savelich says I have to!"

"Tell me—you didn't know about the countess's death when you decided to stay in Moscow?" asked Princess Mary, and immediately blushed, realizing that her question, coming right after his mention of freedom, seemed to attribute motives to him that perhaps he didn't deserve.

"No," Pierre answered, clearly not finding the implied meaning of Princess Mary's words at all awkward. "I heard about it in Orel, and you can't imagine how it shook me. We weren't a model couple," he said quickly, glancing at Natasha and sensing in her curious look a question about what his attitude toward his wife had been. "But that death hit me terribly hard. When two people quarrel, both are always at fault, and your own guilt suddenly becomes unbearably heavy when the other person is no longer alive. And then, such a death... without friends, without comfort. I felt very, very sorry for her," he finished, and was pleased to notice an expression of glad approval on Natasha's face.
"Yes, and so you're an eligible bachelor again," said Princess Mary.
Pierre suddenly flushed crimson and for a long time tried not to look at Natasha. When he ventured a glance her way, her face was cold, stern, and—he thought—even contemptuous.
"And did you really see and speak to Napoleon, as we've been told?" asked Princess Mary.
Pierre laughed.
"No, not once! Everyone seems to think that being a prisoner of war means being Napoleon's guest. I not only never saw him, I never even heard anything about him—I was in much lower company!"
Supper was over, and Pierre, who had at first declined to talk about his captivity, was gradually drawn into doing so.
"But is it true that you stayed in Moscow to kill Napoleon?" Natasha asked with a slight smile. "I guessed it back then, when we met at the Sukharev Tower. Do you remember?"
Pierre admitted it was true, and from there Princess Mary's questions and especially Natasha's gradually led him into giving a detailed account of his adventures.

At first he spoke with the amused, gentle irony that had become his usual manner toward everyone and especially toward himself. But when he came to the horrors and sufferings he'd witnessed, he was carried away without realizing it and began speaking with the restrained emotion of someone reliving painful memories.

Princess Mary looked from Pierre to Natasha with a gentle smile. In the whole story she saw only Pierre and his goodness. Natasha, leaning on her elbow, her expression constantly changing with the story, watched Pierre without taking her eyes off him for a single moment, clearly living through everything he described along with him. From her look, her exclamations and her brief questions Pierre could tell she understood precisely what he wanted to convey. She could follow not only what he said but what he longed to say and could find no words for. This was his account of the child and of the woman he had been arrested for protecting: “It was awful. Abandoned children, some of them in the flames … They snatched one out right in front of me … and women having their things torn off them, their earrings ripped out …” He flushed and grew confused. “Then a patrol came up and they arrested all the men—all the men who weren’t looting, I mean. I was among them.”
"You're not telling us everything—I'm sure you did something..." Natasha said, then paused and added, "something fine?"
Pierre continued. When he reached the execution, he tried to skip over the horrible details, but Natasha insisted that he leave nothing out.
Pierre began to speak about Karataev, then stopped. By this time he had risen from the table and was pacing the room, Natasha following him with her eyes. Then he added:
"No, you can't understand what I learned from that uneducated man—that simple fellow."
"Yes, yes, go on!" said Natasha. "Where is he?"
"They killed him almost before my eyes."
And Pierre, his voice trembling the whole time, went on to tell about the last days of their retreat, Karataev's illness, and his death.

He told his story as he had never recalled it before. He now seemed to see a new meaning in everything he'd been through. And now, telling it all to Natasha, he experienced that pleasure a man feels when women listen to him—not clever women who, when they listen, try to either memorize what they hear in order to enrich their own minds and then repeat it, or to fit what they're told into their own framework and contribute their own clever comments worked out in their own little mental world—but the pleasure that comes from real women, gifted with the ability to select and absorb all that is best in what a man reveals of himself. Natasha, without knowing it, was all attention: she didn't miss a word, a tremor in his voice, a glance, a twitch of his facial muscles, or a gesture. She caught each word on the fly and carried it straight to her open heart, intuiting the mysterious meaning of Pierre's entire spiritual journey.

Princess Mary understood his story and felt for him, but she saw something else now that absorbed all her attention. She saw the possibility of love and happiness between Natasha and Pierre, and this thought, occurring to her for the first time, filled her heart with joy.
It was three in the morning. The servants came in with sad, stern faces to change the candles, but nobody noticed them.

Pierre finished his story. Natasha continued to look at him intently with bright, attentive, animated eyes, as if trying to understand something more that he had perhaps left untold. Pierre, in shy, happy confusion, kept glancing at her and trying to think of something to say that might shift the conversation to a different subject. Princess Mary said nothing. It never occurred to any of them that it was three in the morning and time for bed.

"People talk about misfortunes and suffering," Pierre said, "but if right now someone asked me, 'Would you rather be what you were before you were taken prisoner, or go through it all again?'—for God's sake, let me go through captivity again and eat horseflesh! We imagine that the moment we're knocked out of our usual track, everything is lost. But that's just when something new and good begins. As long as there's life, there's happiness. There's a great deal, a great deal ahead of us. I'm saying this to you," he added, turning to Natasha.
"Yes, yes," she said, answering something quite different. "I too would wish for nothing but to live it all over from the beginning."
Pierre looked at her intently.
"Yes, and nothing more," said Natasha.
"It's not true, not true!" Pierre cried. "I'm not to blame for being alive and wanting to live—and neither are you!"
Suddenly Natasha bent her head, covered her face with her hands, and began to cry.
"What is it, Natasha?" said Princess Mary.
"Nothing, nothing." She smiled at Pierre through her tears. "Good night! It's time for bed."
Pierre got up and said goodbye.
Princess Mary and Natasha met as usual in the bedroom. They talked about what Pierre had told them. Princess Mary didn't say what she thought of Pierre, and Natasha didn't mention him either.
"Well, good night, Mary!" said Natasha. "Do you know, I'm often afraid that by not talking about him"—she meant Prince Andrew—"for fear of not doing justice to our feelings, we're forgetting him."
Princess Mary sighed deeply, acknowledging the justice of Natasha's remark, but didn't say so in words.
"Is it possible to forget?" she said.

"It did me so much good to tell everything today. It was hard and painful, but good—very good!" said Natasha. "I'm sure he truly loved him. That's why I told him... Was it all right?" she added, suddenly blushing.
"You mean telling Pierre? Oh yes. What a wonderful man he is!" said Princess Mary.

"Do you know, Mary..." Natasha suddenly said with a mischievous smile—the kind Princess Mary hadn't seen on her face for a long time—"he's somehow grown so clean, smooth, and fresh—as if he'd just come out of a bath. Don't you think? Out of a moral bath. Right?"
"Yes," Princess Mary replied. "He's improved enormously."
"With a short coat and his hair cropped; just as if—well, just as if he'd come straight from the bath... Papa used to—"
"I understand why he"—meaning Prince Andrew—"loved no one so much as him," said Princess Mary.
"Yes, and yet he's completely different from him. People say men become friends when they're very different. That must be true. He really is nothing like him—in anything."
"Yes, but he's wonderful."
"Well, good night," said Natasha.
And the same mischievous smile lingered on her face for a long time, as if it had been forgotten there.
